tagline: Through mountain towns to the parlor where Coolidge took office
intro: Vermont 100 links the resort towns of Killington and Ludlow, with ski areas on or near the road. This journey begins in Pittsfield, set among the Green Mountains and drained by the Tweed River. At the base of Pico Peak in Killington, Gifford Woods State Park preserves old-growth forest beside Route 100. Farther south, Plymouth Notch occupies a bowl of open fields and woods enclosed by wooded hills, beside the Route 100A branch.

In August 2011, Tropical Storm Irene destroyed sections of Route 100 between Killington and Bethel, preventing vehicle travel into and out of Pittsfield for weeks. Killington was cut off for nineteen days, and Plymouth was also among the Vermont towns isolated by the flooding. The state subsequently reconstructed many segments of Route 100 damaged by the storm.

From Pittsfield, continue south through Killington toward Plymouth and Ludlow. Route 100A offers a branch toward Plymouth Notch and the Coolidge Homestead. The branch runs about seven miles northeast to US 4 in Bridgewater. Back on Route 100, Lake Rescue lies about three miles north of Ludlow’s town center; the village’s former woolen mill marks its industrial history. Okemo Mountain Resort is in Ludlow, at the southern end of this journey.

moments.title: Killington
moments.text: Killington’s name made a return journey in 1999. Chartered as Killington in 1761, the town became Sherburne in 1800, taking the name of landholder Colonel Benjamin Sherburne. Voters chose the original name again in March 1999, and legislative approval made the change effective that July. The ski resort is here, and the Ottauquechee River has its headwaters within the town. Killington Road connects US 4 with the ski area through the central village. North of the village, the Appalachian Trail crosses the town, then joins the Long Trail across its western portion.

moments.title: Coolidge Homestead
moments.text: A family parlor became the setting for a presidential oath at the Coolidge Homestead. Calvin Coolidge was visiting his family here when President Warren G. Harding died. His father administered the oath in the house where Coolidge had lived from age four until leaving for Black River Academy in 1887. His father’s refusal to modernize the house preserved its condition and some furnishings from that night. The inaugural room’s lamp, Bible and table occupy their historic positions behind glass. The restored rooms in Coolidge Hall recall another presidential use: his Summer White House in 1924.

moments.title: Ludlow
moments.text: Ludlow’s three-story brick woolen mill replaced a taller building lost to fire. The first mill opened in 1834, failed during the panic of 1837 and resumed production by 1853. After the 1865 fire came the brick replacement that survives in the village. By 1899, the company employed 130 people and produced 150,000 yards of wool cloth a year. The former mill now houses a condominium and retail businesses within the Ludlow Village Historic District. Elsewhere in the village, Black River Academy, whose alumni included Calvin Coolidge, has housed a local history museum since 1972.
